title: Innate Immunity: Toll-like Receptors and NF-κB

generated.pipeline: extract → Gemini draft → Claude Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Toll-like receptors trigger rapid innate immune responses by freeing {{c1::NF-κB}}, a DNA-binding transcription factor that activates inflammatory genes such as TNF.
cards.quote: Toll-like receptors free NF-κB (a DNA-binding transcription factor that activates inflammatory genes such as tumor necrosis factor, or TNF).

cards.front: Why does injecting a purified foreign protein alone provoke little immunity unless an adjuvant is included?
cards.back: A purified protein lacks microbial molecular patterns that alert innate receptors, whereas an adjuvant supplies an immune-provoking cue.
cards.quote: a purified protein injected alone provokes little immunity without an adjuvant, an additive that provokes the immune system.
cards.section: The idea: detect what a microbe cannot give up

cards.front: How can a short list of pattern-recognition receptors cover microbial threats for which antibodies need billions of variants?
cards.back: Each pattern receptor recognizes an essential feature shared across a whole microbial class and absent from the host, which microbes cannot easily discard.
cards.quote: A pattern receptor fits a whole microbial class that the microbe cannot discard—such as a bacterial lipid coat or viral double-stranded RNA
cards.section: The idea: detect what a microbe cannot give up

cards.front: What central trade-off does canonical TLR–NF-κB signaling manage in innate immunity?
cards.back: TLRs free pre-made NF-κB by destroying its inhibitor; NF-κB drives defense, survival, and brakes to balance protection against host injury.
cards.quote: Toll-like receptors free pre-made NF-κB by triggering inhibitor destruction; NF-κB drives defense, survival and brakes, balancing protection against host injury.
cards.section: The idea: detect what a microbe cannot give up

cards.front: Researchers cloned a human relative of fruit fly Toll and expressed a version locked in its active state in human cells without knowing its ligand. What did activating NF-κB and inflammatory genes show, and what remained unknown?
cards.back: It showed the human Toll relative couples to NF-κB-driven inflammatory gene expression, linking the fly Toll pathway to human innate immunity, while leaving its natural microbial trigger unknown.
cards.quote: In 1997 Ruslan Medzhitov and Janeway cloned a human Toll relative that, locked "on", activated NF-κB and inflammatory genes, though its trigger was unknown.
cards.section: From fly Toll to ten human receptors

cards.front: Lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin), the lipid-and-sugar coat sensed by TLR4, is part of the outer membrane of {{c1::Gram-negative bacteria}}.
cards.quote: lipopolysaccharide (LPS, or endotoxin), the lipid-and-sugar coat of Gram-negative bacteria (those with an outer membrane): the gene was Tlr4.
cards.section: From fly Toll to ten human receptors

cards.front: How does microbial sensing by mammalian Toll-like receptors such as TLR4 differ from that of fruit fly Toll?
cards.back: Fly Toll binds a cleaved host protein after other sensors detect the microbe, whereas mammalian TLRs (with MD-2 for TLR4) bind microbial molecules directly.
cards.quote: Fly Toll does not bind the microbe itself but a host protein cleaved after other proteins sense the microbe
cards.section: From fly Toll to ten human receptors

cards.front: TLRs detect outer microbial molecules at the plasma membrane, whereas they detect microbial nucleic acids inside {{c1::endosomes}}, where ingested cargo is broken open.
cards.quote: outer microbial molecules are read at the plasma membrane, whereas nucleic acids are exposed once swallowed microbes or dying host debris are broken open in endosomes
cards.section: From fly Toll to ten human receptors

cards.front: You discover two pattern-recognition receptors: one binds a bacterial outer-membrane lipid and the other binds viral single-stranded RNA. Where should each sit in a macrophage, and why?
cards.back: The lipid receptor belongs on the plasma membrane to meet intact extracellular bacteria; the viral RNA receptor belongs facing inward inside endosomes, where swallowed virions break open away from host cytosolic mRNA.
cards.quote: The viral RNA receptor belongs inside endosomes, facing inward, where swallowed virions break open away from host cytosolic mRNA.
cards.section: From fly Toll to ten human receptors

cards.front: If a microbe cannot discard an essential surface structure, how can it still evade a Toll-like receptor?
cards.back: It can modify the specific motif the receptor reads—for example, Yersinia pestis makes an altered lipid A at body temperature that TLR4 barely detects.
cards.quote: A microbe cannot discard its outer membrane, but it can modify the motif a receptor reads
cards.section: From fly Toll to ten human receptors

cards.front: Each Toll-like receptor combines a ligand-facing horseshoe of leucine-rich repeats with a cytoplasmic {{c1::TIR domain}} that pairs to dock MyD88.
cards.quote: Each Toll-like receptor has a horseshoe of leucine-rich repeats facing the microbial ligand and a cytoplasmic TIR domain (named for Toll and the interleukin-1 receptor).
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: In LPS-resistant C3H/HeJ mice, TLR4 reaches the plasma membrane and binds LPS with MD-2 normally, but carries a single amino-acid change inside its cytoplasmic TIR domain. Where does signaling fail, and why?
cards.back: Signaling fails at the first intracellular handoff: LPS still pairs the ectodomains, but the damaged TIR domain cannot recruit the adaptors that bring MyD88, so the kinase tower never assembles and NF-κB stays cytoplasmic.
cards.quote: the damaged TIR domain cannot properly gather the adaptors that bring MyD88, so the kinase tower never assembles and NF-κB stays in the cytoplasm.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: How does the MyD88–IRAK helical tower activate the first kinases in the TLR pathway?
cards.back: MyD88 death domains stack with those of IRAK4 and IRAK1 or IRAK2 into a helical tower, packing IRAK4 domains close enough to phosphorylate one another and their IRAK partners.
cards.quote: death domains stack with those of the kinases IRAK4 and IRAK1 or IRAK2 into a helical tower, packing IRAK4 domains close enough to phosphorylate one another
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: Whereas a lysine-48 ubiquitin chain targets a protein to the proteasome, a {{c1::lysine-63}} ubiquitin chain acts as a signaling scaffold.
cards.quote: From ubiquitin and proteolysis, a lysine-48 chain sends a protein to the proteasome, whereas a lysine-63 chain is a scaffold.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: Purified E3 ligase TRAF6, ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme Ubc13/Uev1A, E1, ATP, TAK1–TAB, and IKK are mixed without proteasomes plus wild-type, K48R, or K63R ubiquitin. IKK phosphorylates IκBα with wild-type and K48R ubiquitin, but not K63R. What does this prove?
cards.back: Lysine-63 ubiquitin chains activate IKK without proteolysis, because blocking K63 linkage abolishes IKK activation, blocking K48 linkage has no effect, and no proteasomes are present.
cards.quote: TRAF6, with the two-part enzyme Ubc13/Uev1A, builds lysine-63 chains that activate the IκB kinase complex (IKK).
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: How do lysine-63 ubiquitin chains built by TRAF6 lead to activation of the IKK complex?
cards.back: The TAB2 and TAB3 partners of the kinase TAK1 bind the lysine-63 chain, positioning TAK1 beside IKK to phosphorylate IKK's activation loop.
cards.quote: The TAB2 and TAB3 partners of the kinase TAK1 read the lysine-63 chain, bringing TAK1 beside IKK to phosphorylate IKK's activation loop.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: A mutation prevents TAB2 and TAB3 from binding lysine-63 ubiquitin chains while leaving TRAF6 and the proteasome intact. After LPS arrives, what happens to K63 chains, IKK, IκB, and NF-κB?
cards.back: TRAF6 still builds K63 chains, but TAK1 cannot dock beside IKK; IKK remains off, IκB is not phosphorylated or degraded, and NF-κB stays trapped in the cytoplasm.
cards.quote: TRAF6 still builds lysine-63 chains, but TAK1 cannot dock beside IKK. IKK stays off, IκB is not phosphorylated or degraded, and NF-κB remains trapped in the cytoplasm.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: How does IκB hold pre-made NF-κB inactive in the cytoplasm of a resting cell?
cards.back: IκB binds folded NF-κB and uses its curved ankyrin repeats to cover NF-κB's nuclear localization signal.
cards.quote: NF-κB, a pair of Rel-family proteins, waits folded in the cytoplasm under IκB, whose ankyrin repeats (a curved protein-binding fold) cover NF-κB's nuclear localization signal.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: Phosphorylation of IκBα at serines 32 and 36 by active IKK recruits a second E3 ligase that attaches a {{c1::lysine-48}} ubiquitin chain, sending IκB to the proteasome.
cards.quote: Active IKK phosphorylates IκBα at serines 32 and 36. That mark recruits a second E3 ligase that adds a lysine-48 chain, sending IκB to the proteasome.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: Why does TLR signaling allow NF-κB to enter the nucleus within minutes of touching a bacterium?
cards.back: NF-κB is already synthesized and folded in the cytoplasm; freeing it requires only phosphorylating and degrading IκB, with no transcription or translation needed.
cards.quote: Freed NF-κB enters the nucleus within minutes—no transcription or translation needed.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: List the canonical intracellular steps from a ligand-paired Toll-like receptor to nuclear NF-κB.
cards.back: TLR pair → MyD88 → IRAK4 and IRAK1/2 → TRAF6 → lysine-63 chain → TAK1 → IKK → IκB destroyed → NF-κB enters the nucleus.
cards.quote: TLR pair → MyD88 → IRAK4 and IRAK1/2 → TRAF6 → lysine-63 chain → TAK1 → IKK → IκB destroyed → NF-κB enters the nucleus
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: A macrophage is pretreated with a drug that blocks the proteasome and then stimulated with LPS. What happens to IκB and NF-κB, and why?
cards.back: Phosphorylated, K48-ubiquitinated IκB builds up and NF-κB stays in the cytoplasm, because IKK still marks IκB for destruction but the inhibited proteasome cannot degrade it to release NF-κB.
cards.quote: That mark recruits a second E3 ligase that adds a lysine-48 chain, sending IκB to the proteasome. Freed NF-κB enters the nucleus within minutes—no transcription or translation needed.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: In a cell line lacking baseline NF-κB DNA-binding activity, LPS still induces full NF-κB DNA binding even when protein synthesis is blocked. What does this experiment prove?
cards.back: NF-κB protein already exists in an inactive pool before stimulation, because blocking translation prevents new NF-κB synthesis yet does not prevent activation.
cards.quote: in a cell line lacking the activity, LPS induced DNA binding even with protein synthesis blocked. The protein must already have been there, inhibited.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: Adding detergent to cytoplasmic extracts from unstimulated cells freed active, DNA-binding NF-κB. What did this establish about NF-κB regulation?
cards.back: Inactive NF-κB sits in the cytoplasm held back by a dissociable inhibitory protein (IκB) rather than needing covalent synthesis to become active.
cards.quote: In 1988 Patrick Baeuerle located the inactive pool in the cytoplasm, freed it with detergent, and named IκB.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: Every human Toll-like receptor signals through the adaptor MyD88 except {{c1::TLR3}}, which uses TRIF to drive interferon genes.
cards.quote: First, every TLR uses MyD88 except TLR3, which uses TRIF to drive interferon genes
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: How does TLR4's adaptor usage change when it is internalized from the plasma membrane into an endosome?
cards.back: At the surface TLR4 uses the sorting adaptor TIRAP to recruit MyD88; once internalized into an endosome, it switches to TRIF via the sorting adaptor TRAM.
cards.quote: TLR4 and TLR2 use the sorting adaptor TIRAP to recruit MyD88
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: Macrophages lacking MyD88 are exposed to LPS. Predict the fate of TLR4's surface signaling branch versus its endosomal signaling branch, and state which rules this rests on.
cards.back: Surface TLR4 signaling via TIRAP–MyD88 fails, whereas the endosomal TRIF branch to IRF3 and interferon remains intact. This rests on the rules that surface TLR4 recruits MyD88 via TIRAP, while endosomal TLR4 switches via TRAM to TRIF to drive IRF3 and interferon.
cards.quote: once internalized into an endosome TLR4 switches to TRIF via a second sorting adaptor, TRAM.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: In cells, the IKK subunit NEMO binds {{c1::head-to-tail (linear)}} ubiquitin chains alongside lysine-63 chains so both chain types cooperate to activate IKK.
cards.quote: the IKK subunit NEMO also binds head-to-tail (linear) ubiquitin chains alongside lysine-63 chains, so in cells the two kinds of chain work together.
cards.section: From receptor to gene: three proximity tricks and one destruction

cards.front: How does NF-κB directly terminate its own transcriptional activity in the nucleus?
cards.back: NF-κB switches on the IκBα gene; newly made IκBα enters the nucleus, strips NF-κB off DNA, and carries it back to the cytoplasm.
cards.quote: One gene that NF-κB switches on encodes IκBα, its own inhibitor; new IκBα enters the nucleus, takes NF-κB off the DNA and carries it back out.
cards.section: Ending the response

cards.front: To shut off TLR signaling further upstream of IKK, NF-κB switches on {{c1::A20}}, an enzyme that strips lysine-63 ubiquitin chains.
cards.quote: NF-κB also switches on A20, an enzyme that strips the lysine-63 chains and so shuts the pathway off further upstream.
cards.section: Ending the response

cards.front: Under continuous LPS, a cell degrades its starting IκBα normally, but the NF-κB binding site in the IκBα promoter is deleted. How does nuclear NF-κB behave over time, and why?
cards.back: Initial nuclear entry is normal because releasing pre-made NF-κB needs no transcription; afterward, nuclear NF-κB stays high instead of dropping in waves because no fresh IκBα is made to pull it off DNA.
cards.why: Upstream negative-feedback brakes such as A20 still partially dampen signaling, but the rapid IκBα nuclear-export loop is gone.
cards.quote: without fresh IκBα to pull NF-κB off DNA, nuclear NF-κB stays high instead of dropping in waves (restrained only partially by upstream brakes such as A20).
cards.section: Ending the response

cards.front: A macrophage lacks functional A20 but retains an intact IκBα gene. After LPS stimulation, predict how upstream IKK activity and nuclear NF-κB duration compare with normal cells, and state which rules this rests on.
cards.back: IKK stays active longer and nuclear NF-κB signaling is prolonged. This rests on the rules that lysine-63 chains recruit TAK1 to keep IKK active (driving ongoing IκB destruction) and that NF-κB-induced A20 normally strips those chains as an upstream delayed negative-feedback brake.
cards.quote: These two brakes implement the delayed negative feedback of signaling circuits, driving nuclear NF-κB in waves under a lasting stimulus.
cards.section: Ending the response

cards.front: Why is TNF receptor 1 signaling called "the anti-death, death pathway", and what two checkpoints normally prevent cell death?
cards.back: TNFR1 is a death receptor that normally spares cells via an immediate RIPK1 ubiquitination/phosphorylation brake and a delayed NF-κB-induced survival shield.
cards.quote: the receptor is a death receptor, one that can instruct a cell to kill itself, yet it normally spares the cell.
cards.section: "The anti-death, death pathway": one receptor says die and stay alive

cards.front: Cultured cells express either normal IκBα or an S32A/S36A mutant IκBα that IKK cannot phosphorylate. After 24 h with or without TNF, survival is 95% (−TNF) and 90% (+TNF) for normal IκBα, versus 92% (−TNF) and 22% (+TNF) for mutant IκBα. By what factor does the mutation increase TNF-induced cell death, and why?
cards.back: 14-fold; the mutant IκBα cannot be phosphorylated or degraded, so NF-κB stays trapped and cannot induce survival genes against TNF's death arm. Setup: TNF-induced death with normal IκBα = 95% − 90% = 5%; with mutant IκBα = 92% − 22% = 70%; factor = 70% / 5% = 14.
cards.quote: Survival normally wins; in cultured cells with NF-κB blocked—for instance by an IκBα mutant that cannot be phosphorylated at serines 32 and 36—the same TNF kills.
cards.section: "The anti-death, death pathway": one receptor says die and stay alive

cards.front: Cultured cells with normal IκBα are treated with TNF together with a drug that blocks protein translation. Predict how the delayed and immediate checkpoints are affected and what this means for survival, and state which rules this rests on.
cards.back: Survival is expected to be compromised: the delayed NF-κB shield of newly induced gene products cannot be made when translation is blocked, even though pre-made NF-κB enters the nucleus. Only the immediate RIPK1 brake, which needs no transcription, remains.
cards.quote: Delayed NF-κB survival shield: NF-κB induces genes whose products block the death machinery.
cards.section: "The anti-death, death pathway": one receptor says die and stay alive

cards.front: How does the cytosolic cGAS–STING pathway convert double-stranded DNA detection into interferon gene expression?
cards.back: cGAS binds dsDNA of any sequence and makes cyclic GMP-AMP from GTP and ATP; cyclic GMP-AMP activates ER-bound STING, which moves toward the Golgi, recruits TBK1, and activates IRF3.
cards.quote: cGAS binds double-stranded DNA of any sequence and joins GTP and ATP into cyclic GMP-AMP, a ring second messenger like cAMP.
cards.section: A second alarm: nucleic acid in the wrong place

cards.front: A cell has intact endosomal TLRs (TLR3, TLR7, TLR8, TLR9) and cGAS, but lacks STING. Predict its interferon response to (a) endosomal double-stranded RNA and (b) cytosolic double-stranded DNA, and explain why.
cards.back: (a) Intact, because endosomal dsRNA signals via TLR3 → TRIF → IRF3 without STING. (b) Lost, because cytosolic dsDNA triggers cGAS to make cyclic GMP-AMP, which cannot activate TBK1 and IRF3 without STING.
cards.quote: It binds STING in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane; activated STING moves toward the Golgi, recruits the kinase TBK1, and activates IRF3 to switch on interferon genes
cards.section: A second alarm: nucleic acid in the wrong place

cards.front: A young child suffers recurrent Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae infections with minimal fever. Isolated blood cells fail to make cytokines when challenged with bacterial lipoproteins or flagellin, yet still induce interferon in response to endosomal double-stranded RNA. Which signaling defect best fits, and which rules explain this pattern?
cards.back: Loss of MyD88 (or IRAK4, with MyD88 matching adaptor wiring directly). This rests on the rules that bacterial lipoproteins (TLR2) and flagellin (TLR5) require MyD88 whereas endosomal dsRNA (TLR3) uses TRIF, and that MyD88/IRAK4 deficiency causes recurrent pus-forming bacterial infections with little fever.
cards.quote: Children lacking working MyD88 or IRAK4 suffer repeated, severe infections with pus-forming bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus, often with little fever
cards.section: Too little and too much

cards.front: How can circulating bacterial LPS cause septic shock during a severe Gram-negative infection?
cards.back: Circulating LPS triggers widespread TNF and inflammatory mediators that widen and leak blood vessels, dropping blood pressure and injuring organs.
cards.quote: In some Gram-negative infections, circulating LPS triggers widespread TNF and other mediators that widen and leak blood vessels, dropping blood pressure and injuring organs in septic shock.
cards.section: Too little and too much

cards.front: LPS-blind mice survive a dose of purified endotoxin that kills normal mice, yet die far more easily from a live Gram-negative bacterial infection. How does the core balancing rule of TLR–NF-κB signaling explain both outcomes?
cards.back: Without LPS sensing, mice avoid lethal host-driven inflammatory shock from purified endotoxin, but cannot mount the NF-κB defense needed to clear replicating bacteria. This rests on the rule that TLR–NF-κB signaling balances antimicrobial protection against host injury.
cards.quote: Much injury comes from the host's own alarm—and LPS-blind mice show both sides, resisting purified endotoxin yet dying far more easily from live Gram-negative infection.
cards.section: Too little and too much

cards.front: In clinical trials, drugs blocking TLR4 or TNF have not improved survival in human sepsis. Which properties of human sepsis and TLR signaling explain why?
cards.back: The lesson gives these facts: human sepsis is broader than Gram-negative endotoxin shock, combines inflammatory injury with immune suppression, and LPS-blind mice die more easily from live infection, so blocking an innate alarm can cost host defence.
cards.quote: Human sepsis is broader than endotoxin shock: it often lacks a Gram-negative cause, combines inflammatory injury with immune suppression, and drugs blocking TLR4 or TNF have not improved patient survival.
cards.section: Too little and too much

cards.front: How does monophosphoryl lipid A answer Janeway's 1989 adjuvant puzzle for licensed vaccines against HPV and shingles with far less toxicity than intact LPS?
cards.back: It is a modified LPS fragment that activates TLR4 to provoke innate immunity for the vaccine while producing far less inflammatory toxicity than intact LPS.
cards.quote: Monophosphoryl lipid A, a modified LPS fragment activating TLR4 with far less toxicity, serves as part of the adjuvant in licensed vaccines against human papillomavirus and shingles
cards.section: Too little and too much

cards.front: Two identical DNA oligonucleotides are delivered into macrophage endosomes: one carries unmethylated CG sequences and the other carries methylated CG sequences. Which activates the endosomal DNA sensor TLR9, and why?
cards.back: The unmethylated CG oligonucleotide activates TLR9, because unmethylated CG motifs are common in bacterial and many viral DNAs, whereas CG sequences in host DNA are scarce and usually methylated.
cards.quote: TLR9 binds DNA in which the sequence CG is unmethylated. That is common in bacterial DNA and in many viral DNAs
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: People born lacking TREX1, a nuclease that clears DNA from the cytosol, develop Aicardi-Goutières syndrome without any viral infection. Predict the signaling state of their cells and state which rule of cytosolic DNA sensing explains it.
cards.back: Their cells make interferon nonstop, producing inflammation resembling a congenital viral infection. This rests on the rule that cGAS binds double-stranded DNA of any sequence and stays quiet only if host DNA is kept out of the cytosol and cleared.
cards.quote: People who lack TREX1, a nuclease that clears DNA from the cytosol, develop an inflammatory disease, Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, that resembles a viral infection present from birth.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Adult fruit flies with a disabled Toll pathway failed to express the antifungal peptide drosomycin and died after Aspergillus fumigatus infection, even though Toll binds the cleaved host protein Spatzle rather than the fungus directly. What did this show?
cards.back: It showed that the developmental gene Toll is also required in adult flies for inducible antifungal defense, acting downstream of microbial sensors via a protease-activated host ligand.
cards.quote: Bruno Lemaitre showed that adult flies with a disabled Toll pathway failed to express the antifungal peptide drosomycin and died after Aspergillus fumigatus infection.
cards.section: Toll in the fly, in full

cards.front: Positional cloning in two independently LPS-tolerant mouse strains revealed a single cytoplasmic amino-acid substitution in Tlr4 in C3H/HeJ mice and complete loss of Tlr4 in C57BL/10ScCr mice. What does obtaining the same LPS-unresponsive phenotype from both alleles confirm?
cards.back: It confirms that Tlr4 is the essential gene for LPS sensing—eliminating the receptor or disabling its cytoplasmic signaling domain both abolish the LPS response.
cards.quote: C3H/HeJ mice carried one cytoplasmic amino-acid substitution, whereas C57BL/10ScCr mice had lost Tlr4 entirely.
cards.section: Cloning Tlr4, in full
